opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it wasn't a sudden decision; it came out of the work I'd been doing for years.

My background is in computer vision and generative models, things like GANs, image and video generation, and 3D. Over time I kept running into the same question: we can generate very realistic pixels, but does the model actually understand the world? Can it predict what happens when you push something, open a door, or pick up a cup? Visual generation started to look less like the end goal and more like a stepping stone toward world models, and the natural place a world model has to prove itself is in physical action. That's embodied intelligence.

Timing was the second factor. A few years ago, if you wanted to work on robots, the bottleneck was everywhere: hardware was expensive, data was scarce, and the models weren't general enough. Now large models have shown that scaling data and compute gives you real generalization, hardware costs are dropping fast, and there's a lot of energy in the supply chain, especially in China. It felt like the window where a foundation-model approach to robotics could actually work, rather than hand-engineering one task at a time.

The third factor was the environment. Embodied AI is a long game. You need patience, sustained investment, and a team that can work across models, data, and hardware. Building this inside a group like Ant, with the resources and the long-term orientation to treat it as foundational research rather than a quick product, made it possible to take the bigger bet. We could focus on the core problems, like data, the base model, and how perception, reasoning, and action come together, instead of chasing a demo.

Personally, I also just think it's one of the most important open problems right now. Language models have gone very far in the digital world, but most of the economy and most of daily life is physical. If AI is going to really help people, it eventually has to act in the real world. So there was some risk in switching directions, but it felt like the right problem at the right time, and I'd rather spend these years on something that hard than on something safe.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a single moment of decision. It was more like a slow accumulation of restlessness.

I'd spent years on generative models, on vision, on getting machines to produce images and video that look convincing. And at some point I realized the thing I was building was very good at seeing the world and describing it, but it couldn't do anything in it. It was all perception, no consequence. You generate a beautiful frame, and then what? Nothing moves.

For me, the appeal of embodied intelligence is that it closes that loop. The model has to act, the world pushes back, and you find out immediately whether your understanding was real or just plausible. In pure generative work you can fool yourself for a long time. A robot arm will not let you fool yourself. It drops the cup.

As for why Ant, and why Lingbo specifically, I think a few things mattered. One was that I wanted to be somewhere with a real appetite for a long bet. Embodied AI is not a six-month product cycle. The data is scarce, the hardware is fragile, the evaluation is messy. You need an organization willing to tolerate that for years. Another was the people. I'd worked with some of them before, and I trusted that we shared a sense of what "good" looks like, which matters more than almost anything when the field is this early and there's no established recipe.

And I'll be honest, there was also some ego in it. Vision generation had become crowded. Everyone was doing it, the gaps were narrowing, and I felt I'd said most of what I had to say there. Embodied intelligence felt like the place where the questions were still genuinely open, where a small team could still change the shape of the problem rather than just inch the benchmark forward.

Was I certain? No. I'm still not certain. But I'd rather be uncertain about something that matters than confident about something that's already been mostly solved.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal of embodied intelligence is that it brings perception, reasoning, and action together. It’s one thing for a model to describe a situation; it’s another for a robot to act in that situation, observe what changes, and adjust. That interaction with the physical world is a very compelling research problem.

So I would frame the decision around two questions: Is this a direction worth committing to for the long term? And can we build a team where research and engineering move forward together? That’s how I think about pursuing embodied intelligence at Ant Lingbo—working toward systems whose intelligence is demonstrated through what they can actually do.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the appeal of embodied intelligence is that it brings perception, reasoning, and action together. Understanding an image or generating a video is valuable, but having a system act in the physical world—and learn from the consequences—introduces a different set of challenges.

So I thought about the decision in terms of that whole loop. How do we connect what a model understands with what a robot can actually do? And when something goes wrong, how does that experience help the system improve? Pursuing embodied intelligence at Ant Lingbo was a way to focus on those questions and work toward capabilities that are useful in real environments.
